name: Timor-Leste
headline: Timor-Leste's Constitution promises access to personal data, but no data protection law is in force and a draft only went to consultation in August 2026.

access.summary: Article 38 of the Constitution gives citizens a right of access to personal data in computer and manual records, but the law meant to set its conditions does not exist. We found no right to a copy of a medical record and no patient portal.
detail: Article 38(1) of the 2002 Constitution says all citizens have the right of access to personal data about them, in computer or manual records, and may demand correction and know the purpose. Article 38(2) leaves the definition and conditions to an ordinary law.
Law 10/2004 on the Health System, Article 7, gives users the right to be informed of their condition and treatment options. It does not grant a copy of the clinical file.
A 2004 decree on private health units requires a register of every patient and says records must stay confidential without prejudice to the patient's right to information about their own situation.

The August 2026 draft data protection law would add a free right of access (Article 15), answered without undue delay but with no fixed deadline. It is not law yet. We found no national or provider patient portal.
Score: no enforceable right in ordinary law, and the constitutional right covers citizens only, so the cell sits in the 15 to 35 band.

control.summary: The Constitution bans computer processing of private-life data without consent, and the health law lets patients refuse care. There is no data law, no consent tool and no access log, so the Ministry of Health decides how records are used.
detail: Article 38(3) of the Constitution expressly bans computer processing, without consent, of personal data on private life, political and philosophical beliefs, religion, party or union membership and ethnic origin. Health is not named separately.
Law 10/2004, Article 7(1)(b), lets users decide whether to accept proposed care, and Article 7(1)(d) gives a right to have personal data kept confidential.
No data protection law is in force and no regulator exists to enforce consent rules, as a March 2026 academic review confirms.
The 2026 draft would allow health data processing without consent for medical purposes by a professional bound by secrecy. We found no patient-facing consent setting or access log.

privacy.summary: Timor-Leste has no data protection law and no data protection authority. A draft law creating an independent authority with fines up to USD 150,000 was in public consultation from 1 to 30 August 2026.
detail: The Constitution protects privacy (Article 36) and personal data (Article 38), but the implementing law has never been passed. A March 2026 review found no data protection law and no independent authority as of January 2026.
The Penal Code (Decree-Law 19/2009), Article 184, punishes revealing a secret learned through one's profession with up to 1 year in prison or a fine, on complaint.

The Ministry of Justice opened consultation on a draft law on 1 August 2026. It treats health as sensitive data, creates an independent Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados and sets fines of USD 5,000 to 150,000 for companies in the most serious cases.
A cybersecurity package sent to Parliament on 31 July 2026 also covers data protection rules. We found no reported health data breach. Score: constitutional and penal protection only, no regulator.

commercial.summary: No law limits selling health data or using it for marketing, and no regulator could act on it. The 2026 draft law would make unlawful sale or disclosure of personal data a very serious offence when intentional or when health data is involved.
detail: Without a data protection law, the only general limits are the constitutional consent rule for private-life data and the Penal Code secrecy offence.

Article 39 of the draft data protection law lists unlawful communication, disclosure, sale or handing over of personal data to third parties as a very serious offence when intentional or when it involves sensitive data such as health data.
We found no rules on data brokers, de-identified health data sales or consumer health apps.

journey.summary: Public health programmes run on a national DHIS2 system with patient-level tracking for TB, HIV, malaria, hypertension and diabetes. Individual digital immunization records only began as a 12-facility pilot in Dili in 2026.
detail: The Timor-Leste Health Information System (TLHIS) runs on DHIS2 and is the country's main health management backbone, WHO and the UN say.
A case-based electronic system for TB, HIV and malaria launched in November 2023 to replace paper records gradually. Patient-level tracking has since expanded to hypertension and diabetes.

In May 2026 an immunization e-Tracker pilot started at 12 Dili facilities, described as the country's first move to individual-level digital immunization records. Before it, vaccinators wrote each child into three separate paper registers.
In 2018 the government said Saúde na Família had built electronic family health profiles for over one million people. Whether that registry is still in use was not verified.

clinical.summary: The health law calls for confidential exchange of clinical information between care levels, but we found no shared record that clinicians can open across facilities.
detail: Law 10/2004, Article 6(2), requires close links between care levels and a permanent, confidential exchange of clinical information about users.

In 2018 the Health Minister said the Saúde na Família electronic record was individual and could be used across the territory to give professionals each person's history. Current use was not verified.
The new DHIS2 trackers serve disease programmes. We found no evidence that hospital doctors can see primary care or laboratory records from other facilities.

research.summary: No consent rule or opt-out governs secondary use of health data. A Ministry of Health ethics office reviews research and trial protocols, and the Penal Code punishes breaches of professional secrecy.
detail: Score: base 40 for no consent and no opt-out, plus 3 for statutory professional secrecy and 3 for an ethics review body, held at 45 (lower half of the band) because the ethics office's current operation was not verified.

Ministerial Diploma 1/2014 gives the Office of Ethics and Quality Control the task of reviewing research protocols and clinical trial requests in National Health Service facilities. Whether it still runs under the current ministry structure was not verified.
Law 10/2004, Article 13, says clinical trials will be covered by a specific law with multidisciplinary approval committees. We found no such law.
Article 23 of the 2026 draft data law leaves research rules to future guidance from the new authority.

ai.summary: No rules for clinical AI exist. A Ministry of Health TB van already uses AI to read chest X-rays, with health workers responsible for decisions as a matter of practice, not law.
detail: WHO reported in August 2026 that a Ministry of Health mobile TB van uses portable digital X-ray with AI that flags images needing attention.
A partner said health workers remain responsible for interpretation and clinical decisions. This is a stated practice, not a legal requirement.
WHO's 2025 country profile lists pharmaceutical laws still in draft. We found no device rules covering AI software.
A Digital Transformation Strategy 2026-2036, in consultation in April 2026, includes a regulatory framework for AI. It is not adopted.
